judgments.reasoning_cat1: The recitals are narrative and mostly definite, though "approximately 266,200 square feet" and "most advantageous site ... all factors considered" are loose descriptive language rather than operative promises. Nothing here needs a boundary drawn for a party's obligation, so intrinsic risk is modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The fourth recital describes a "no-cost assignable option," which sits slightly against the operative $10.00 consideration clause and against Optionor's cost-bearing obligations in §§5, 6 and 12; that is a possible recital-versus-operative tension but not a squarely contradictory one.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Approximately 10.89 acres" and the reliance on Exhibit 1 for the legal description leave the subject matter only loosely fixed, and "for the price and within the time specified in this Option" imports the indefinite term of §2. "Fully assignable at any time prior to closing to Optionee's developer" is also open as to whether the class of permitted assignees is limited to a developer.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exhibit 3 ¶1 recites "containing 10.89 acres" without "approximately" and identifies the description in Attachment A rather than Exhibit 1, and §13 states a broader assignment right than the "to Optionee's developer" limit here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Shall continue in effect for a period of not less than one (1) year" sets a floor with no ceiling, so the outer date of the option — and hence when it can still be exercised — cannot be fixed from the words; the reference to "its expiration" presupposes an expiry the clause never supplies. That is a named, genuine ambiguity of the kind parties litigate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read against §14 (termination on failure to exercise "within the time ... provided herein"), §21 (time of the essence), and the thirty-day extension right, the missing outer limit produces an unreconcilable gap about the option's life.
judgments.clause_name: Paragraph 2 — Term of Option (exercise by written notice)

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The mechanism turns on "the annual tax incremental financing reimbursement received by Developer" and on an illustrative example, leaving unclear whether the $1,000,000 balance is an absolute obligation or contingent on TIF receipts, and who owes it (Optionee or Developer). "Standard deductions and prorations" and "deductions as described below" add further boundary uncertainty.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be read with §4 (conveyance "upon payment of the Purchase Price, less the Outstanding Balance"), §8 and §12's deductions from the Outstanding Balance, and §12's retention of the balance by Optionee — a web that leaves the payment obligor and timing genuinely uncertain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Good and marketable indefeasible fee simple title ... free and clear of all liens and encumbrances whatsoever, subject only to those items ('Permitted Exceptions') set forth in Exhibit 1" is definite in form, but the parenthetical defines Permitted Exceptions by reference to Exhibit 1 alone.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: §6's second paragraph defines "Permitted Exceptions" differently — as conditions not objected to or accepted by Optionee — so the same defined term carries two sources, and conveyance to "the Developer" assumes an assignment that §13 makes optional.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The obligations and deadlines are specific, but the phrase "necessary to affect the Optionee's desired street closures by December 31, 2006" is syntactically ambiguous as to whether the date fixes delivery of the survey or the closures, and "such Table A items as Optionee may elect" leaves scope open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coheres with §12's street-vacation obligations and §5's Exhibit 2 attachment; no contrary provision was found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause suddenly uses "Seller" and "Purchaser," terms never defined in this agreement, and requires a policy "in the amount of the purchase price" while also demanding it "without standard exceptions" — a mechanical slip plus an undefined-term problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The second sentence duplicates the thirty-day delivery deadline of the first with slightly different wording ("as soon as possible"), and Exhibit 1 is the document where a Seller/Purchaser vocabulary would belong.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Either (1) ... (2) ... (3)" offers three alternatives under a word suited to two, and option (2) is drafted as a verb phrase ("allow Optionor to attempt") that does not parse with "Optionee shall have the option of"; "unable or unwilling" also blurs the trigger.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supplies a second, different definition of "Permitted Exceptions" from the one in §4 keyed to Exhibit 1, and its cure window runs "during the term of the Option," which §2 leaves open-ended.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Record owner" and "requisite power and authority" are settled conveyancing terms and the representation is short and unqualified. Nothing needs construing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with §22's authority documentation requirement and the LLC identification in the preamble.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The representation mixes an unqualified statement ("possession ... has been peaceable and undisturbed") with knowledge-qualified ones, so the extent of the knowledge qualifier across the sentence is not perfectly clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits with §7's closing sentence on continuing truth and with Schedule A exceptions, though Schedule A is expressly carved out only from ¶7(e).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Of sufficient size, capacity" measured "for its current use" is vague and arguably self-defeating, since the deal contemplates a new 266,200 sq. ft. federal facility rather than current use; "without any special charge, assessment or apparatus" is also loosely bounded.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read against the recital describing the intended federal office facility and §12's utility-relocation approvals, the "current use" limitation sits awkwardly with the contemplated development.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "All environmental information that it has" is a definite, if broad, undertaking, and the "facility" definition is anchored to MCL 324.20101; the wording is workable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly carved out of the ¶7(e) representations and dovetails with §8's Due Care regime, so it harmonises with the whole.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "To the best of Optionor's actual knowledge" is a standard qualifier and the compliance representation, though broad, is textually clear about its subject matter and time period.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Schedule A and ¶7(d) carve-outs are expressly stated, so it reconciles with the acknowledged "facility" status.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list "storage, disposal, deposit, treatment, or recycling" is enumerated without a catch-all, and "toxic, dangerous or hazardous substances" is undefined here, leaving "dangerous" without a statutory anchor.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is reconciled with ¶7(d)'s admission that the property is a "facility" by the express "except ... as described in paragraph 7(d)" preface.
judgments.clause_name: 7(e)(2). No Storage or Disposal of Hazardous Substances

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The sentence "The exemptions include that owner's obligations to comply with its due care requirements" is garbled — exemptions do not "include" obligations — and the representation is conditioned on a hypothetical future purchaser availing itself of exemptions, so its operative content is hard to pin down.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interacts with §8's Due Care cost allocation and the $500,000 Limitation of Liability without stating how the representation and that cap relate.
judgments.clause_name: 7(e)(3). No Activities Subjecting Owner to Liability

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The bring-down is short and clear in form, but "until and including any exercise of this Option" borrows the open-ended duration problem and leaves the period between exercise and closing uncovered.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Against §2's indefinite term and §9's ninety-day post-exercise closing, the representations' survival to closing is left unaddressed.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Reasonably cooperate," "most cost effective and appropriate," "best efforts" and "maximum allowable reimbursable costs" are all standard-of-effort phrases with no defined boundary. Whether any of them was breached would be a question of construction plus fact.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits consistently with §12's allocation of Brownfield drafting to Optionor and Eligible Activity identification to Optionee, though the split of estimating responsibility is stated twice in slightly different terms.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "The unapproved amount not to exceed $500,000" is numerically definite, but "all of the costs and activities necessary to achieve Due Care both during pre and post construction" leaves the measurement of the unapproved shortfall imprecise.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: §12's later paragraph imposes a further deduction "up to the Limitation of Liability" for under-approved Eligible Activity costs, raising a real question of double-counting against the same $500,000 cap and the same Outstanding Balance.
judgments.clause_name: 8. Limitation of Liability for Unapproved Due Care Costs

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "No later than 90 days after exercise of this Option" is a hard, computable deadline and the venue is delegated to Exhibit 1. The wording is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It presupposes exercise "by Optionee or its Developer," whereas §2 speaks only of Optionee serving notice, a small mismatch with the assignment mechanics of §13.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The second sentence is ungrammatical ("Optionee will have an opportunity to inspect the Property and that the Property will be conveyed"), and "as is" condition "except as otherwise provided" leaves the carve-out's reach uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The "as is" conveyance stands against the affirmative environmental and utility representations in §7 and the Due Care cost allocation in §8, a tension a court would have to harmonise.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: After enumerating test borings, plans, surveys and environmental assessments, the clause adds "any other due diligence matters deemed reasonably prudent" — a classic catch-all whose reach against the specifics is uncertain, and "reasonable notice" is undefined.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits with §5's survey and §8's Phase II work and is bounded by "during the period of this Option," consistent with the rest of the instrument.
judgments.clause_name: 11. Optionee's Right to Enter and Inspect the Property

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list of approvals is prefaced "may include, but not be limited to," yet Optionor's cost responsibility is then limited to street vacations and zoning variances, leaving allocation of the unlisted approvals (utility relocation, site plan, special use permit) open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Later paragraphs of §12 add Optionor duties for the Brownfield Plan and traffic studies, so the boundaries of "at Optionor's expense" must be pieced together across the section.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "As soon as practical" and "a final determination of those costs" are undefined triggers, and the sixty-day disagreement window depends on that undefined determination date.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The termination right here sits alongside §14's termination-on-non-exercise and the indefinite term in §2, but they are not contradictory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Optionee will use its best efforts to secure funds to reimburse" is a soft, government-appropriation-flavoured obligation whose content is uncertain, and "reasonable documented expenses" is bounded only by the $50,000 cap.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The condition keys to whether "Developer does not execute the Purchase and Sale Agreement," which meshes with §13's optional assignment but leaves the case where no Developer is ever designated unaddressed.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Provide its support and written consent when required" leaves both the trigger and the content of "support" undefined, and the second sentence's "on the Optionee's behalf" is an unexplained agency concept.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The agency language sits awkwardly with §15's statement that neither party is the other's agent, a specific tension worth noting.
judgments.clause_name: 12. Optionor's Support and Consent for Approvals

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Reasonable and necessary to affect Optionee's intended use" and the split of who determines Eligible Activities "with the assistance of" the other are loose but conventional cooperation formulas.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It largely repeats §8's estimating allocation, and the two passages describe the responsibility in slightly different terms without contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Obtain approval of the Brownfield Plan for the project prior to Optionee by no later than December 1, 2006" is garbled — "prior to Optionee" has no object — so the obligation's content is uncertain on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The four thirty-day extensions can push performance past dates assumed elsewhere (§5's December 31, 2006 survey; §21's time-of-the-essence), and §12's later paragraph contemplates closing without an approved plan.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "That amount (up to the Limitation of Liability) shall be deducted" is ambiguous as to whether "that amount" is the approved sum or the shortfall between agreed and approved costs — the two readings produce opposite results.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps the §8 deduction against the same $500,000 cap and the same Outstanding Balance, and the fault carve-outs must be squared with §8's mutual best-efforts duty.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "The Outstanding Balance shall be retained by Optionee" presupposes Optionee holds funds, whereas §3 defines the balance as sums payable out of TIF reimbursements received by the Developer over years — the retention mechanic is not intelligible on its own terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It conflicts in practical operation with §3's instalment payment scheme and §4's conveyance "upon payment of the Purchase Price, less the Outstanding Balance," and with §12's deduction paragraphs.
judgments.clause_name: 12. Retention of Outstanding Balance Pending Approval

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "This Option may be assigned by the Optionee, without the consent of the Optionor" is unrestricted as to assignee, while the rest of the paragraph assumes the assignee is a "Developer"; "in it sole discretion" is also a typographical slip.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: §1 limits assignability to "Optionee's developer" prior to closing, so the two provisions describe different assignment rights and must be reconciled.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Elects not to exercise" plus "within the time and in the manner provided herein" makes termination depend on a time that §2 never fixes; whether the clause requires an affirmative election or operates automatically on lapse is also open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its operation depends entirely on §2's "not less than one (1) year" term, and it is the only termination mechanism in the instrument, so the gap in §2 is inherited here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause contains obvious typographical corruption ("ferninine", "particular portion I which such word is used") but the intended meaning of these boilerplate construction rules remains recoverable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The no-agency statement is in mild tension with §12's reference to Optionor obtaining approvals "on the Optionee's behalf," though the rest of the instrument is consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Any other additional instruments ... as may be necessary" and "in the form and substance satisfactory to the parties and their respective counsel" combine an open-ended duty with a mutual veto, so the obligation's content is uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coheres with §16's release-on-termination purpose and §18's amendment formality; no contrary provision found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard counterparts language with no undefined or ambiguous term. The wording is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the execution blocks and the rest of the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause names this Option, Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 3 as the only agreements, but the following sentence says all undertakings are "embodied in this Option and Exhibit 1," dropping Exhibit 3 — an internal inconsistency within the clause itself.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exhibit 2 (survey) and Schedule A (representation exceptions) are made parts of the agreement by §5 and §7(e) yet are omitted from the integration list, leaving their status uncertain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "All disputes arising under or relating to this Option shall be resolved under this Act" is clear in scope, and the Contracting Officer is named; the only softness is "[e]xcept as provided in the Act."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the federal-party structure of the instrument and with §20's notice addressee; no competing dispute mechanism appears.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Delivery methods and deemed-receipt rules are specified for mail and courier but not for personal delivery, leaving a gap in when personally delivered notice is "received" — significant because §2 makes exercise effective on receipt.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: §2 and Exhibit 3 ¶2 both make the exercise date turn on receipt "as provided in Section 20," so the omitted personal-delivery rule matters to the option's central mechanic.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The time-of-the-essence formula is conventional and the weekend/holiday rule is precise; nothing internal requires construction.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is hard to reconcile with §2's "not less than one (1) year" open-ended term and with the "as soon as practical" and extendable deadlines in §§6 and 12, where time is expressly elastic.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause requires a resolution or, "if the Optionor is a general or limited partnership," general-partner approval and the partnership agreement — it enumerates entity types that omit the limited liability company Optionor actually is, so which document is owed is unclear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The preamble and Exhibit 3 identify Optionor as a Limited Liability Company signed by a Managing Member, so the enumerated entity forms do not match the party described elsewhere.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Purely identificatory recital of parties, dates and addresses; the only defect is OCR-level punctuation. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches the main agreement's preamble, including the August 1, 2006 Effective Date.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The grant is stated in past tense ("granted") for recording purposes and is otherwise clear, though "the price and within the time specified in this Option" imports the undefined outer term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It says the Property contains "10.89 acres" and is described in Attachment A, whereas §1 says "approximately 10.89 acres" described in Exhibit 1 — a discrepancy in the description of the same land across recorded and unrecorded documents.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It repeats "not less than one (1) year from the Effective Date" with a reference to "its expiration" that the text never fixes, so the recorded instrument gives the public no ascertainable outer date for the option. That is the same named ambiguity as §2 and is squarely litigable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates §2 of the main agreement and depends on §20 for notice, so the indefinite-duration problem is reproduced in the instrument given public notice, compounding the §14 termination question.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single-purpose recording statement; "to give public notice that the Optionee or its assignee has the right to purchase the Property" is plain. Nothing ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with §13's assignment right and with the recording instructions at the head of Exhibit 3.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit 3, 3. Purpose of Memorandum of Option Agreement
